\chapter{Learning Theory — CCE}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from TCSlib.LearningTheory.Minimax.CCE
\section{Overview}

This module develops the theory of \emph{coarse correlated equilibria} (CCE)
for finite two-player games.  It introduces joint distributions over action
profiles, defines (approximate) CCE in terms of one-sided deviation utilities,
constructs the empirical joint distribution from a sequence of mixed-strategy
plays, and proves the main result: if both players run no-regret algorithms
with per-round external regret at most $\varepsilon$, then their empirical
joint distribution is an $\varepsilon$-CCE.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Two-player finite game]
\lean{Game}
\label{Game}
\leanok
A finite two-player game with $M$ row actions and $N$ column actions, specified
by a row utility function $u_r : \mathrm{Fin}\,M \times \mathrm{Fin}\,N \to \mathbb{R}$
and a column utility function $u_c : \mathrm{Fin}\,M \times \mathrm{Fin}\,N \to \mathbb{R}$.
Both players are utility maximizers.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Embedding a zero-sum game]
\lean{ZeroSumGame.toGame}
\label{ZeroSumGame.toGame}
\leanok
\uses{Game, ZeroSumGame}
Given a zero-sum game $G$ with payoff matrix $A$, this embeds it into the
general two-player framework by setting the row utility to $A$ and the column
utility to $-A$, so that both players are maximizers of their respective
utilities.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Joint distribution over action profiles]
\lean{JointDistribution}
\label{JointDistribution}
\leanok
A joint distribution $\sigma$ on $\mathrm{Fin}\,M \times \mathrm{Fin}\,N$ is a
nonnegative function $\sigma_{ij} \ge 0$ satisfying
$\sum_{i,j} \sigma_{ij} = 1$.  It represents a correlated distribution over
pure action profiles of the two players.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Row marginal]
\lean{JointDistribution.rowMarginal}
\label{JointDistribution.rowMarginal}
\leanok
\uses{JointDistribution}
The row marginal of $\sigma$ at row action $i$ is
$\sigma^{\mathrm{row}}_i = \sum_{j} \sigma_{ij}$,
i.e.\ the probability that the row player plays $i$ under $\sigma$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Column marginal]
\lean{JointDistribution.colMarginal}
\label{JointDistribution.colMarginal}
\leanok
\uses{JointDistribution}
The column marginal of $\sigma$ at column action $j$ is
$\sigma^{\mathrm{col}}_j = \sum_{i} \sigma_{ij}$,
i.e.\ the probability that the column player plays $j$ under $\sigma$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Nonnegativity of the row marginal]
\lean{JointDistribution.rowMarginal_nonneg}
\label{JointDistribution.rowMarginal_nonneg}
\leanok
\uses{JointDistribution, JointDistribution.rowMarginal}
\difficulty{1}
Let $\sigma$ be a joint distribution on $\mathrm{Fin}\,M \times \mathrm{Fin}\,N$, so
$\sigma_{ij} \ge 0$ for all $i,j$ and $\sum_{i,j} \sigma_{ij} = 1$. Then for every row
action $i$ the row marginal $\sigma^{\mathrm{row}}_i = \sum_{j} \sigma_{ij}$ satisfies
$\sigma^{\mathrm{row}}_i \ge 0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Nonnegativity of the column marginal]
\lean{JointDistribution.colMarginal_nonneg}
\label{JointDistribution.colMarginal_nonneg}
\leanok
\uses{JointDistribution, JointDistribution.colMarginal}
\difficulty{1}
Let $\sigma$ be a joint distribution on $\mathrm{Fin}\,M \times \mathrm{Fin}\,N$, and
let $j$ be a column action. Then the column marginal $\sigma^{\mathrm{col}}_j = \sum_{i}
\sigma_{ij}$ satisfies $\sigma^{\mathrm{col}}_j \ge 0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Row marginals sum to one]
\lean{JointDistribution.rowMarginal_sum_one}
\label{JointDistribution.rowMarginal_sum_one}
\leanok
\uses{JointDistribution, JointDistribution.rowMarginal}
\difficulty{1}
Let $\sigma$ be a joint distribution over $\mathrm{Fin}\,M \times \mathrm{Fin}\,N$, and
for each row action $i$ let $\sigma^{\mathrm{row}}_i = \sum_{j} \sigma_{ij}$ denote its
row marginal. Then the row marginals sum to one:
\[
\sum_{i} \sigma^{\mathrm{row}}_i = 1.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Column marginals sum to one]
\lean{JointDistribution.colMarginal_sum_one}
\label{JointDistribution.colMarginal_sum_one}
\leanok
\uses{JointDistribution, JointDistribution.colMarginal}
\difficulty{2}
Let $\sigma$ be a joint distribution on $\mathrm{Fin}\,M \times \mathrm{Fin}\,N$. Then
the column marginals sum to one: $\sum_{j} \sigma^{\mathrm{col}}_j = 1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}[Row expected utility]
\lean{JointDistribution.rowExpectedUtility}
\label{JointDistribution.rowExpectedUtility}
\leanok
\uses{Game, JointDistribution}
The row player's expected utility under $\sigma$ in game $G$ is
$\sum_{i,j} \sigma_{ij} \cdot u_r(i,j)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Column expected utility]
\lean{JointDistribution.colExpectedUtility}
\label{JointDistribution.colExpectedUtility}
\leanok
\uses{Game, JointDistribution}
The column player's expected utility under $\sigma$ in game $G$ is
$\sum_{i,j} \sigma_{ij} \cdot u_c(i,j)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Row deviation utility]
\lean{JointDistribution.rowDeviationUtility}
\label{JointDistribution.rowDeviationUtility}
\leanok
\uses{Game, JointDistribution, JointDistribution.colMarginal}
The row player's expected utility from unilaterally deviating to the fixed
pure action $i'$, while the column player keeps $\sigma$'s column marginal:
$\sum_{j} \sigma^{\mathrm{col}}_j \cdot u_r(i', j)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Column deviation utility]
\lean{JointDistribution.colDeviationUtility}
\label{JointDistribution.colDeviationUtility}
\leanok
\uses{Game, JointDistribution, JointDistribution.rowMarginal}
The column player's expected utility from unilaterally deviating to the fixed
pure action $j'$, while the row player keeps $\sigma$'s row marginal:
$\sum_{i} \sigma^{\mathrm{row}}_i \cdot u_c(i, j')$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Coarse correlated equilibrium]
\lean{IsCoarseCorrelatedEquilibrium}
\label{IsCoarseCorrelatedEquilibrium}
\leanok
\uses{Game, JointDistribution, JointDistribution.rowDeviationUtility, JointDistribution.rowExpectedUtility, JointDistribution.colDeviationUtility, JointDistribution.colExpectedUtility}
A joint distribution $\sigma$ is a \emph{coarse correlated equilibrium} (CCE)
of game $G$ if neither player can improve their expected utility by committing
in advance to any fixed pure action: for all $i'$,
$\mathrm{rowDevUtil}(\sigma, G, i') \le \mathrm{rowExpUtil}(\sigma, G)$, and
for all $j'$, $\mathrm{colDevUtil}(\sigma, G, j') \le \mathrm{colExpUtil}(\sigma, G)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$\varepsilon$-coarse correlated equilibrium]
\lean{IsApproxCoarseCorrelatedEquilibrium}
\label{IsApproxCoarseCorrelatedEquilibrium}
\leanok
\uses{Game, JointDistribution, JointDistribution.rowDeviationUtility, JointDistribution.rowExpectedUtility, JointDistribution.colDeviationUtility, JointDistribution.colExpectedUtility}
A joint distribution $\sigma$ is an \emph{$\varepsilon$-coarse correlated
equilibrium} ($\varepsilon$-CCE) of game $G$ if each player's gain from any
unilateral pure deviation is at most $\varepsilon$: for all $i'$,
$\mathrm{rowDevUtil}(\sigma, G, i') \le \mathrm{rowExpUtil}(\sigma, G) + \varepsilon$,
and similarly for the column player.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Exact coarse correlated equilibrium is approximate]
\lean{IsCoarseCorrelatedEquilibrium.toApprox}
\label{IsCoarseCorrelatedEquilibrium.toApprox}
\leanok
\uses{Game, IsCoarseCorrelatedEquilibrium, IsApproxCoarseCorrelatedEquilibrium, JointDistribution, productDistribution}
\difficulty{2}
Let $G$ be a finite two-player game with $M$ row actions and $N$ column actions, and let
$\sigma$ be a joint distribution over the action profiles $(i,j)$ that is a coarse
correlated equilibrium of $G$; that is, neither player can increase their expected
utility under $\sigma$ by committing in advance to a fixed pure action, so that for
every row action $i'$ the row player's utility from deviating to $i'$ (against the
column marginal of $\sigma$) is at most their expected utility under $\sigma$, and
likewise the column player's utility from deviating to any fixed action $j'$ (against
the row marginal of $\sigma$) is at most their expected utility under $\sigma$. Then for
every real $\varepsilon \ge 0$, the distribution $\sigma$ is an $\varepsilon$-coarse
correlated equilibrium of $G$: each player's gain from any such unilateral pure
deviation exceeds zero by at most $\varepsilon$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}[Product distribution]
\lean{productDistribution}
\label{productDistribution}
\leanok
\uses{JointDistribution, MixedStrategy}
Given mixed strategies $p$ for the row player and $q$ for the column player,
the product (independent) joint distribution assigns to each profile $(i,j)$
the probability $p_i \cdot q_j$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Row marginal of a product distribution]
\lean{productDistribution_rowMarginal}
\label{productDistribution_rowMarginal}
\leanok
\uses{JointDistribution.rowMarginal, MixedStrategy, productDistribution}
\difficulty{2}
Let $p$ be a mixed strategy for the row player over $M$ actions and $q$ a mixed strategy
for the column player over $N$ actions, and let $\sigma$ be their product distribution,
so that $\sigma_{ij} = p_i q_j$ for every profile $(i,j)$. Then for each row action $i$
the row marginal of $\sigma$ equals the corresponding weight of $p$, that is, $\sum_{j}
p_i q_j = p_i$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Column marginal of a product distribution]
\lean{productDistribution_colMarginal}
\label{productDistribution_colMarginal}
\leanok
\uses{JointDistribution.colMarginal, MixedStrategy, productDistribution}
\difficulty{2}
Let $p$ be a mixed strategy over $M$ actions for the row player and $q$ a mixed strategy
over $N$ actions for the column player, and let $\sigma$ be their product distribution,
which assigns probability $p_i\,q_j$ to each pure profile $(i,j)$. Then for every column
action $j$, the column marginal of $\sigma$ at $j$ equals $q_j$; that is, $\sum_{i}
p_i\,q_j = q_j$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}[Empirical joint distribution]
\lean{empiricalJoint}
\label{empiricalJoint}
\leanok
\uses{JointDistribution, MixedStrategy}
Given $T > 0$ rounds of play in which the row player uses mixed strategy $p_t$
and the column player uses $q_t$, the empirical joint distribution assigns to
each profile $(i,j)$ the time-averaged probability
$\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} (p_t)_i \cdot (q_t)_j$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Row marginal of the empirical joint distribution]
\lean{empiricalJoint_rowMarginal}
\label{empiricalJoint_rowMarginal}
\leanok
\uses{JointDistribution.rowMarginal, MixedStrategy, empiricalJoint}
\difficulty{3}
Fix $T \ge 1$ rounds of play in which the row player uses mixed strategies
$p_1,\dots,p_T$ over $M$ actions and the column player uses mixed strategies
$q_1,\dots,q_T$ over $N$ actions, and let $\sigma$ be the empirical joint distribution,
which assigns to each profile $(i,j)$ the time-averaged probability
$\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} (p_t)_i (q_t)_j$. Then for every row action $i$, the row
marginal $\sigma^{\mathrm{row}}_i = \sum_{j} \sigma_{ij}$ equals the time-average of the
row player's weight on $i$:
\[
\sigma^{\mathrm{row}}_i \;=\; \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} (p_t)_i .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Column marginal of the empirical joint distribution]
\lean{empiricalJoint_colMarginal}
\label{empiricalJoint_colMarginal}
\leanok
\uses{JointDistribution.colMarginal, MixedStrategy, empiricalJoint}
\difficulty{3}
Consider $T > 0$ rounds of play between a row player with $M$ actions and a column
player with $N$ actions, where in round $t$ the row player uses the mixed strategy $p_t$
over the row actions and the column player uses the mixed strategy $q_t$ over the column
actions. Form the empirical joint distribution $\sigma$ assigning to each profile
$(i,j)$ the time-averaged probability $\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} (p_t)_i (q_t)_j$. Then
for each column action $j$, the column marginal $\sigma^{\mathrm{col}}_j = \sum_i
\sigma_{ij}$ equals the time-average of the column player's weights on $j$,
\[
\sigma^{\mathrm{col}}_j = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} (q_t)_j.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Averaging a payoff against the empirical joint distribution]
\lean{empiricalJoint_sum_prob_mul}
\label{empiricalJoint_sum_prob_mul}
\leanok
\uses{MixedStrategy, empiricalJoint}
\difficulty{4}
Fix $T > 0$ rounds of play in which, in round $t$, the row player uses a mixed strategy
$p_t$ over $\mathrm{Fin}\,M$ and the column player a mixed strategy $q_t$ over
$\mathrm{Fin}\,N$; write $(p_t)_i$ and $(q_t)_j$ for the weights placed on actions $i$
and $j$. Let $\sigma$ be the empirical joint distribution, whose value at each profile
$(i,j)$ is the time average $\sigma_{ij} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} (p_t)_i\,(q_t)_j$.
Then for every function $f : \mathrm{Fin}\,M \times \mathrm{Fin}\,N \to \bbr$,
\[
\sum_{i}\sum_{j} \sigma_{ij}\, f(i,j) \;=\; \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i}\sum_{j}
(p_t)_i\,(q_t)_j\, f(i,j).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Row expected utility of the empirical joint distribution]
\lean{empiricalJoint_rowExpectedUtility}
\label{empiricalJoint_rowExpectedUtility}
\leanok
\uses{Game, JointDistribution.rowExpectedUtility, MixedStrategy, empiricalJoint, empiricalJoint_sum_prob_mul}
\difficulty{1}
Fix a finite two-player game with $M$ row actions and $N$ column actions, and write
$u_r(i,j)$ for the row player's payoff at the pure profile $(i,j)$. Suppose that over $T
> 0$ rounds the row player plays a mixed strategy $p_t$ and the column player a mixed
strategy $q_t$ in each round $t$, and let $\sigma$ be the empirical joint distribution
given by $\sigma_{ij} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}(p_t)_i\,(q_t)_j$. Then the row
player's expected utility under $\sigma$ equals the time-average of the per-round
bilinear payoffs:
\[
  \sum_{i,j}\sigma_{ij}\,u_r(i,j)
    = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i,j}(p_t)_i\,(q_t)_j\,u_r(i,j).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Column utility of the empirical joint distribution]
\lean{empiricalJoint_colExpectedUtility}
\label{empiricalJoint_colExpectedUtility}
\leanok
\uses{Game, JointDistribution.colExpectedUtility, MixedStrategy, empiricalJoint, empiricalJoint_sum_prob_mul}
\difficulty{1}
Consider a finite two-player game with $M$ row actions and $N$ column actions, whose
column payoff is $u_c(i,j)$ for the action profile $(i,j)$. Fix $T \ge 1$ rounds in
which the row player plays the mixed strategy $p_t$ and the column player plays the
mixed strategy $q_t$, and let $\sigma$ be the empirical joint distribution, which
assigns to each profile $(i,j)$ the time-averaged probability $\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}
(p_t)_i\,(q_t)_j$. Then the column player's expected utility under $\sigma$ equals the
time-average of the per-round bilinear column payoffs:
\[
  \sum_{i=1}^{M}\sum_{j=1}^{N} \sigma_{ij}\, u_c(i,j)
  = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\sum_{j=1}^{N} (p_t)_i\,(q_t)_j\, u_c(i,j).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Empirical row deviation utility as a time average]
\lean{empiricalJoint_rowDeviationUtility}
\label{empiricalJoint_rowDeviationUtility}
\leanok
\uses{Game, JointDistribution.rowDeviationUtility, MixedStrategy, empiricalJoint, empiricalJoint_colMarginal}
\difficulty{3}
Let $G$ be a finite two-player game with $M$ row actions and $N$ column actions, and let
$u_r(i,j)$ denote the row player's utility. Fix an integer $T \ge 1$, and suppose that
in each round $t \in \{1,\dots,T\}$ the row player plays the mixed strategy $p_t$ over
the $M$ row actions and the column player plays the mixed strategy $q_t$ over the $N$
column actions, giving rise to the empirical joint distribution $\sigma$ with
$\sigma_{ij} = \tfrac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} (p_t)_i\,(q_t)_j$. Then for every pure row
action $i'$, the row player's deviation utility under $\sigma$ equals the time average
of the expected utilities of playing $i'$ against each round's column strategy:
\[
  \sum_{j} \sigma^{\mathrm{col}}_j\, u_r(i',j)
  = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{j} (q_t)_j\, u_r(i',j).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Column deviation utility of the empirical joint distribution]
\lean{empiricalJoint_colDeviationUtility}
\label{empiricalJoint_colDeviationUtility}
\leanok
\uses{Game, JointDistribution.colDeviationUtility, MixedStrategy, empiricalJoint, empiricalJoint_rowMarginal}
\difficulty{3}
Let $G$ be a finite two-player game with $M$ row actions and $N$ column actions and
column utility $u_c(i,j)$, and fix a number of rounds $T \ge 1$. Suppose that in each
round $t \in \{1,\dots,T\}$ the row player plays a mixed strategy $p_t$ over the $M$ row
actions and the column player plays a mixed strategy $q_t$ over the $N$ column actions,
and let $\sigma$ be the empirical joint distribution that assigns mass
$\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} (p_t)_i\,(q_t)_j$ to each action profile $(i,j)$. Then, for
every column action $j'$, the column player's expected utility from deviating to the
pure action $j'$ against the row marginal $\sigma^{\mathrm{row}}_i = \sum_{j}
\sigma_{ij}$ is the time average of the round-by-round deviation utilities:
\[
  \sum_{i} \sigma^{\mathrm{row}}_i\, u_c(i,j')
  = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i} (p_t)_i\, u_c(i,j').
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[No-regret play yields an approximate coarse correlated equilibrium]
\lean{empiricalJoint_isApproxCCE}
\label{empiricalJoint_isApproxCCE}
\leanok
\uses{Game, IsApproxCoarseCorrelatedEquilibrium, MixedStrategy, empiricalJoint, empiricalJoint_rowDeviationUtility, empiricalJoint_rowExpectedUtility, empiricalJoint_colDeviationUtility, empiricalJoint_colExpectedUtility}
\difficulty{4}
Let $G$ be a finite two-player game with row utility $u_r$ and column utility $u_c$ over
$M$ row actions and $N$ column actions, and consider $T > 0$ rounds of play in which the
row player uses the mixed strategy $p_t$ and the column player uses the mixed strategy
$q_t$ at round $t$. Fix $\varepsilon \in \bbr$, and suppose that for every pure row
deviation $i'$,
\[
  \sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{j}(q_t)_j\, u_r(i',j)
  \;-\; \sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i,j}(p_t)_i (q_t)_j\, u_r(i,j)
  \;\le\; \varepsilon T,
\]
and for every pure column deviation $j'$,
\[
  \sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i}(p_t)_i\, u_c(i,j')
  \;-\; \sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i,j}(p_t)_i (q_t)_j\, u_c(i,j)
  \;\le\; \varepsilon T.
\]
Then the empirical joint distribution of the play, which assigns to each profile $(i,j)$
the probability $\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}(p_t)_i (q_t)_j$, is an $\varepsilon$-coarse
correlated equilibrium of $G$.
\end{theorem}
